Muslims across the world celebrate two Eids respectively
known as Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha.
Eid-ul-Fitr is a festival that marks the end of Ramadan,
the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. During the holy
month of Ramadan, Muslims do not eat or drink
anything during daylight hours. Eid-ul-Fitr, therefore,
celebrates the end of a month of fasting. Its name means
"Festival of Breaking Fast" in Arabic.
Muslims begin the festival by praying together at dawn
on the first day. Later, families gather to enjoy special
meals and sweets. Children wear new clothes, and gifts
m/Employee
are exchanged. People also visit the graves of their
relatives. Some cities hold elaborate outdoor ceremonies.
Eid-ul-Adha is an important festival in Islam. It is held
each year to commemorate Hazrat Ibrahim's (y)
devotion to Allah (,) and his readiness to sacrifice his
son, Hazrat Ismail ().
The name Eid-ul-Adha means "Festival of Sacrifice" in
Arabic.
It is a time for prayer, visiting with friends and family, and
giving gifts. Many families also sacrifice an animal in
commemoration of Hazrat Ibrahim's (ruw) sacrifice.
Then they distribute the meat among family members,
friends, neighbours, and the poor.
